In spite of competition the Waverley Theater holds its ground. A neat and pretty little theater as our readers, doubtless, are aware. Last night it was made merry by the production of "Ixion" burlesque, well known to this public, and justly admired as a bit of nonsense. The piece was put upon the stage with neat scenery and very careful manner. The performance of it did not equal that previously given here by the Lydia Thompson Troupe; yet it was a performance replete with vivacity and glow. Mr. Rogers the Pierrot was delicious, a representative of broad, affected, grotesque absurdity. Miss Jennie Wilmore is pretty and pleasing as Pixie. The part of Jupiter was filled by Mrs. Sedley Browne, whose beauty and spirit made the character particularly effective. Mr. Dunn acted Dionysus, and his vocalism was as sweet and agreeable as ever. The general cast of the piece attracted general commendation. A couple of dances, by the Rig girls, were greeted with cordial appreciation. "Ixion" is one of the best of burlesques because it is simple, unpretending, and genuine absurdity; and when it was last night at the Waverley Theater, it afforded a great deal of amusement to the people, and in this sultry summer weather that has suddenly come upon us—it cannot fail, we imagine, to please the numerous admirers of burlesque.


THE TAMMANY.

A voluptuous dance by a young lady in red caters, succeeded. Then ensued the chief sensation of the evening. A graceful, slender, agile young woman proceeded, on the trapeze and other contrivances, by perilous flights and dashes in mid-air, to imperil her life in a manner sufficiently audacious to thrill the most hardened sinner. But the star of the evening was Corinda by Mr. W. Lefingwell, whose delineations proved irresistible this occasion and took with rapture the whole audience, keeping the house in roar at every fresh display of his remarkable graces. Those wretched mortals who imagine that Count John, one of the most notorious and idiosyncratic Bohemians of Gotham, is dead, are miserably mistaken. He is alive, and, if not actually kicking, would like to be executing that toe-and-heel performance upon the persons of various New York editors whom he construes into having libelled him. Indeed, it is dangerous to say anything about Count Johannes in print—dangerous, at least for those puny-souled editors who live in terror of libel suits. The Count has as keen a scent for libel as a crow has for carrion; and where the libellous paragraph is, there will Count Johannes be found gathered together. While so engaged in contemplating these abusive columns, his appearance is striking, not to say awful and profound. He wears yellow straw hat, bound with a black tape border, a black bombazine-looking coat and his morid and furrowed complexion is framed in with a wig, the positive degree of which would be brown, the comparative auburn, the superlative red. PENDINGTON, Dec. 7.

Presbytery has closed, and its last regular meeting is held at Newberry Courthouse. Methodist camp-meeting commenced yesterday at Sandy Springs, five miles from this place, to continue during the week. We had quite frost in the low lands this morning, but not enough to do any damage. The session of the criminal side of the Circuit Court for Anderson closed this evening, Judge presiding. There were twelve convictions, two of the parties indicted pleading guilty; of these one only was white. The rest being negroes. The cases were of varying gravity; one of burglary, three or four grand larceny, two petty larceny, and the rest of petty thefts. The sentences were imprisonment at the penitentiary for various terms not exceeding two years. In most of the cases for assault the parties were discharged from imprisonment upon paying costs and small fines.

ST. LOUIS REPUBLICAN.


Our Indian affairs are rapidly assuming a shape which nearly compromises the honor of the American people. We allude particularly to the recent battle in which the Chief Black Kettle, his village, and a large portion of his warriors, were destroyed by the military force under command of Gen. Sheridan and Custer. It would certainly seem as if one fact ought to be, and could effectually settled beyond any doubt or cavil. Sheridan, in his report of Jan. 1, claims that he simply did his duty in the premises, and that there are no mitigating circumstances which should inspire us with any emotions of pity for the unfortunate beings who were sent to swift and bloody doom. Mr. President, in concluding these remarks, I desire to say that I am no volunteer. For several years I have carefully avoided saying anything on this most irritating question, being anxious that negotiators should be left undisturbed to secure a settlement which could be accepted by a deeply injured nation. The submission of the pending treaty to the judgment of the Senate left no alternative. It became my duty to consider it carefully in Committee, and to review the whole subject. I failed to find what we had right to expect, and, if the just claims of our country assumed unexpected proportions, it was not because I would bear hard on England, but because I wish most sincerely to remove all possibility of strife between our two countries, and it is evident that this can be done only by first ascertaining the nature and extent of difference. In this spirit I have spoken to-day.

If the case against England is strong, and if our claims are unprecedented in magnitude, it is only because the conduct of this power at a trying period was most unfriendly, and the injurious consequences of this conduct were on a scale corresponding to the theatre of action. Life and property were both swallowed up, leaving behind a deep-seated sense of enormous wrong, as yet unatoned and even unacknowledged, which is one of the chief factors in the problem now presented to the statesmen of both countries. The attempt to close this great international debate without complete settlement is little short of puerile. With the lapse of time and with minister considerations the case against England becomes more grave, not only from the questions of international responsibility which it involves, but from the better comprehension of the damages which were during the war and for some time thereafter impossible to state thus. The mass of a mountain cannot be measured at once. The observer must occupy a certain distance. As this rule of perspective is justly applicable to damages which are vast beyond measure, a few dates will show the progress of the controversy and how the case enlarged. Going as far back as the 20th of November, 1862, we had our minister in London, Mr. Adams, asking for redress from the British Government on account of the Alabama. This was the mild beginning. On the 22d of October, 1863, in another communication the same minister suggested to the British Government any an equitable form of arbitration or reference.

This proposition languished in the British Foreign Office for nearly two years, whilst the Alabama was pursuing her piratical career, when on August 30, 1865, it was answered by Lord Russell, only to be knocked down in these words:

"...your letter of Oct 9, 1863, we are pleased to say that the Government of the United States is ready to agree to any form of arbitration."

Her Majesty's Government must, therefore, either to make reparation and compensation for the captures made by the Alabama, or to refer in question to any foreign state.

Such was our repulsion from England, which, at least, has the merit of frankness, if notting else. On the 11th of October, 1865, our minister informed Lord Russell that the United States had duly resolved to make no effort for arbitration. Again the whole question slumbered until the 11th of August, 1866, when Mr. Seward presented a list of individual claims on account of the interests Alabama. From that time this question has continued with ups and downs. Until at last the pending treaty was signed.

Had the early overtures of our Government been promptly accepted, or had there been in time last recognition of the errors, I doubt not that this great question would have been settled; but the rejection of our very moderate propositions and the protracted delay, which afforded an opportunity to review the case in its enlarged bearings, have awakened the people to the magnitude of the interests involved. Our demands are larger now than our heirs. It is not the only time in history when such a rise has occurred. The story of such a repulse is repeated, and England is thus a man hanging. Shall these claims be ignored and cancelled promptly, or allowed to simmer until called into activity by some later exigency? There are many among us who, taking counsel of sense of national wisdom, would wish it to rest without a precedent to furnish precedent to others. Who, invoking the counsel of perseverance, would spur them absolutely on. Others who, invoking the counsel of prudence, would assert that England will not honor it. As a question from both sides, it is no doubt one of our country's most important.

Whenever any combinations or conspiracies as defined by the law of the United States of July 31st, 1861, to define and punish certain conspiracies, may be organized and directed against the laws or officers of the State of Texas, the offenders shall upon conviction by a military commission, be subject to the same penalties as are prescribed by that law, and it is made the duty of all Magistrates and peace officers having a knowledge of any such combination or conspiracy to report it to the Post Commander.

4. Whenever any prisoner shall break or escape from any penitentiary, Jail or other place of penal confinement, or from the custody of any Sheriff or other officer after having been duly arrested, the fact will be immediately reported to the Post Commander, setting forth the name of the escaped prisoner, his age, residence, and description, the crime for which he was committed, and whether under conviction or awaiting trial, and any other fact that may lead to his apprehension. A like report will be made in the case of all persons against whom warrants have been issued, who have fled or otherwise evaded arrest. In all such cases it shall be the duty of the Post Commander to issue his warrant for the arrest of the criminal wherever he may be found within the limits of his post.

5. Sheriffs of counties and marshals of cities and towns, (when the municipality is independent of the county organizations) whenever any felony or other grave crime has been committed within the limits of their respective jurisdictions, will immediately report the fact to the Post Commander, giving the nature of the crime, the name of the person against whose person or property it was committed, and, if known, the name, residence, and occupation of the offender. Whenever any person, so reported, has been arrested, the Post Commander will be notified of the fact.

6. On the first day of each month, Sheriffs of counties and Marshals of cities and towns, and all other peace officers, not included in the force of any Sheriff or Marshal, will make to the Post Commander a consolidated report of all crimes committed, and of all arrests made within the limits of their respective jurisdictions during the preceding month. The first report made to include the period from the 1st of January, 1869, to the date of the report. Post Commanders will forward the consolidated reports to District Headquarters, retaining a copy, and will add thereto a report of crimes committed within the limits of their posts, and not included in the reports of Sheriffs and Marshals, and a report of all arrests made by military authority during the same period.

7. The Clerks of the Courts of Criminal Jurisdiction in this State will as soon as practicable, report to these Headquarters the name, residence, and description of all persons under indictment for felony or other grave crimes, who have forfeited their bail or failed to appear for trial.

8. The Sheriffs of counties and Marshals of cities and towns will as soon as practicable report to these Headquarters the condition of the jails or other places of confinement under their charge, as to capacity, and security, and whether any repairs or improvements are needed to make them secure. They will also report whether adequate provision is made by the county or town for the care and maintenance of the prisoners who may be confined in them.

9. Whenever any Magistrate, Clerk, Sheriff, or other civil officer, is required to perform any service not devolved upon them by the laws of the State, he will be allowed and paid from the reconstruction funds the same fees or compensation as now allowed by law for similar services. The accounts for such services will be forwarded through the Post Commander, for his approval or remarks, except when the service is required from District Headquarters, in which case they will be sent direct.

ST. PETERSBURG, RUSSIA, Feb. 8, 1869.

of the United States Volunteer Army,
being in St. Petersburg, coming well
recommended by distinguished citizens
of the United States, and being also well
educated, and of good address, I called
upon the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and
told him that I would not apply in the
usual way by note to have Captain Ches-

Imperial Majesty would be disposed to
act, but desired that he would approach
his Imperial Majesty in an informal way,

We have report of most revolving
case of rape, which occurred near Ere.
mont, Obion county, Tennessee, last
week, upon the person of little girl,
only seven or eight years of age, by the
name of Sheffield, by man by the name
of Dennis. Dennis, it appears, took an
opportunity when there was no one about
the house but the little girl, and forcibly
accomplished his desires. The little girl
told her relations of the affair, and her
injuries fully confirmed her charges.
Dennis was arrested by the District Con-
stable and taken before Esquire Caldwell,
who refused to entertain the charges
because he could not receive the little
girl as competent witness on account
of her age. Dennis, we understand, has
left the country, but that officers and
citizens are now actively on the lookout
for his re-arrest.


P.S.-Since writing the above we hear
that the little girl has died from the inju-
ries received. The citizens pursuing
Dennis overlook him near Double
Bridges, Dyer county, Tennessee, and it
is generally understood they killed him.
Hickman Courier, 1871.

It is to call attention briefly to few plain
homely truths, that may be as familiar as
household words, but it is well to consider
occasionally subjects, and give warnings,
even at the risk of being charged with
presenting thoughts that have been re-
iterated thousand times. None are more
responsible for silence on the great curse

the Press. The great curse of the present

men among the young men from sixteen

of intemperance is rapidly on the increase.
Not desiring to discuss at this time the
current temperance, issues of license or no
license and whatever may be the views of
any citizen upon those subjects, there is
not an honorable man, whether temper.
ance man in the strict sense of the term or
not, if he looks around and considers
where the young men of the present day
are standing but can be alarmed at their
peril. Let us all appeal to the sober
Judgment and candid good sense of the

When the vice of inebriety has taken
fast hold of man, farewell to industry,
farewell emulation, farewell love of good
society, farewell decency of manner and
oivilities of life. Everything noble in
the aspirations of the soul, is sunk in a
predominant appetite. How many in
stances are before our eyes daily of men
who began life with the highest prospects
before them who have closed it without
a ray of comfort or consolation. Young
men with good fortunes, fine talents, mild
tempers, kind hearts, vigorous constitu-
tious, being drawn into the vortex of the
incorporates, have become by degrees the
most loathsome of mankind. In the home
of the intemperate, there is no happiness.
All is uncertainty and anxiety,-his out
goings and incoming, are unknown.
When he will labor or rest, is wholly a
matter of chance His life becomes one
of pain, as sure as night brings morning.
Poverty and misery are in the train. In
avoiding these shoals, no man is called
upon to make a sacrifice, and no aid to
accomplish it. His own will is all that is
requisite.


Friends of the young men OF to-day,
rally around them with all the power of
wholesome, moral suasion, and with rea-
son and kindness, avoid all force and i'll
temper, and win the hope of the State,
and of the republic from the paths of in
ebriety, and save them from contempt,
disgrace and misery, that they may be
rescued from the great curse of the land,
to honorable and useful lives, to take the
places of the fathers who are so rapidly
passing from the stage of active life, and
most of them to the grave.

civilities of life. Everything noble in
the aspirations of the soul, is sunk in a
predominant appetite. How many in
stances are before our eyes daily of men
who began life with the highest prospects
before them who have closed it without
a ray of comfort or consolation. Young
men with good fortunes, fine talents, mild
tempers, kind hearts, vigorous constitu-
tions, being drawn into the vortex of the
inebriates, have become by degrees the
most loathsome of mankind. In the home
of the intemperate, there is no happiness.
All is uncertainty and anxiety,—his out-
goings and incomings, are unknown.
When he will labor or rest, is wholly a
matter of chance. His life becomes one
of pain, as sure as night brings morning.
Poverty and misery are in the train. In
avoiding these shoals, no man is called
upon to make a sacrifice, and no aid to
accomplish it. His own will is all that is
requisite.

Friends of the young men of to-day,
rally around them with all the power of
wholesome, moral suasion, and with rea-
son and kindness, avoid all force and ill
temper, and win the hope of the State,
and of the republic from the paths of in-
ebriety, and save them from contempt,
disgrace and misery, that they may be
rescued from the great curse of the land,
to honorable and useful lives, to take the
places of the fathers who are so rapidly
passing from the stage of active life, and
most of them to the grave.

We never did like cats. When in infancy we strayed, our delight was to capture the ancient tabby, that slumbered in peace and sunshine on the doorstep, and chew on it with our infant teeth. As we grew older our dislike to them increased. We couldn't endure a catechism, even, We disliked cats. And as for Pussyism, it never found favor with us.

The first time we ever got a black eye was all on account of a cat. There lived near our native vale an Italian Countess named Bridget Mahoney, who had retired from the world and sought life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness far away from her aristocratic connections, with many others of her exiled compatriots, on a classic region known as Vinegar Hill. She had strapping boys and a lean, wall-eyed gray cat. This fine, high-spirited animal was of the feminine gender, and accustomed to attend assemblages of her sex, and attend nightly conventions of the Female Cats Rights Association, that met on the woodshed attached to the next house to ours. When high words passed between the members, and when, as was not unfrequently the case, a wretch of masculine cat came spying about, and calling for his "Murrier-Murrier," she would pounce upon the screant and make the law.

The point of her arguments generally told with effect.

Now this incompatible and accomplished Tabby had enemies among her own as well as the opposite sex. She was hated because of her eloquence and power. Among her enemies was 'the youth of calm demeanor, mischievous propensities and torn trousers' whose room was reached from the woodshed where those feline arguments of the Female Cats Association were made. The number of shoebrushes, bosties, sticks and stones that boy and his partner, who lived next door, threw at those cats were incalculable.

One night the discussion grew so hot that it was determined by the two boys to break it up. Cleverly their plans were laid. They procured a nice piece of meat and fastened it to string, running the string to the bedroom window.

Everything being fully prepared, the result was awaited impatiently.

At the regular hour of ten o'clock the Female Cats Rights Association commenced assembling. One of the first to come was Tabby. Cautiously she approached the bait, smelt it, and, in a few seconds, bolted it string and all. We had her on string then. She sputtered and spitted and got her back up about it, but it was of no avail. We had the cat where the hair was short. Hauling her into the pillow-case we had prepared in lieu of bag, we went over to the neighborhood of the residence of Mrs. Mahoney, and tying a pack of fire crackers to the cat's tail, we touched them off and let her go.

Every time one of those crackers were discharged Tabby was rolled over endwise. Away she went, now running, now rolling, through hole in the door of the Countess' castle, the crackers popping and swapping like a young Fourth of July.

From the Augusta (Ga.l Chronicle.


In one of the mountain counties of
Georgia there lives two families, each be-
fore the war noted for its wealth and re-
fnement Since the war the families
(whom we shall call respectively Il and u,
though they had, like nearly everybody
else, lost everything by the conflict, still
retained the high position in society which,
they had for some long time filled. One of
them, the LIS, lost several of its members,
as well as its fortune, By the war, and at
the time of our story consisted of Mr..
i, gentleman 30 years of age, his wife,
nearly the same age, and an unmarried
daughter of about %. Within about
quarter of mile of their house lived one
of the RS, q young man who had recently.
married q very beautiful young lady of the
county, and having left the paternal man.
sion, was farming by himself on a small
tract of ground. The two families lived
some distance from the county town, in
sparsely inhabited section of country, and,
being each the nearest neighbor of the
other. were, of course, on terms of great
intimacy. Between the young wife and
the daughter of Mr.. l.. fast friendship
was soon formed.


A few days since Mr.. r. informed his
wife that he had received letter, which
would compel immediate attendance in At
lanta, where he would have to remain sew
eral days, and as it would be inconyenient
for him TO take her with him 10 that CITY.
| advised that she should ask her young
neighbor to stay with her during his alb
sence. The next morning he set out in his
| buggy for Atlanta, and his wife during the
morning went over to j.. s for the purpose
| of inviting her young friend to stay wit her.
The young lady. after consultation with
her mother, readily assented to the propo-
sition, and promised to come over during
| the afternoon.


About O'Clock Mrs. r. began to feel a
little uneasy, as Miss l.. had not yet come,
when a servant came up to the house and
brought note from her expected friend,
stating that she would be unable to spend
the night with her, as she had promised. for
her father, from some cause or other, had
positively refused to give his consent to the
arrangement After delivering the note
the servant took his departure, and the
brave woman prepared to spend the night
by herself. Feeling that she had protec-
tor N a large and very fierce yard-dog be-
longing TO her husband, she took him into
her bedroom, and after securing the house
lay down and resigned herself to sleep.


About II o'clock she was awakened from
her slumbers by noise in the house and
the angry growing of the dog, and discov-
cred that the hall door had been forced,
and that some one was standing OF her
room door, seeking an entrance. Speaking
as loudly as her fright would let her, Mrs.
R asked, ''Who is there ?" 4 mans
voice, which she did not recognize, replied
by telling her to ''open the door" Again
she asked the same question, and again re-
ceiyed the same answer, the stranger adding
that if she refused he would ''break the
door down." During this dialogue the dog,
still growing, crouched upon the floor as if
ready TO spring. Thinking to intiniidate
this man, who sought her ruin, Mrs. R.
cried to him that if he forced the door she
would shoot him.


Laughing scornfully, tho rufian threw
his weight against the light door, burst it
open and entered the room-when, quick
as thought, the savage dog sprang forward
and fastened on Lis neck. The man. Gsi ga
ished at this sudden attack, attempted TO
kill the animal with knife which he held
in his hand, but unsuccessfully, and the
powerful animal dragged him to the
ground, still retaining his hold upon his
throat. Stunned at first by this unlocked
for deliverance, the woman in q few Sec
onds, regaining her presence of mind some
what, ran screaming from the house never
stopping until she arrived at the place of
the LIS, where her cries soon aroused the
family.


Her tale was rapidly told, and the servants
were preparing to go to the scene of dan
ger, when suddenly Mr.. l.. was missed,
and his wife almost on the instant as if
struck by a sudden presentiment, screamed
''Merciful God it must be my husbandr
With cry OF horror the party set forth,
and run as fast to the house of Mrs. II. as
the latter had run away from ita few min
utes before. Arrived there they found the

From the Augusta (Ga.) Chronicle.


In one of the mountain counties of
Georgia there lives two families, each before the war noted for its wealth and re-
finement. Since the war the families
(whom we shall call respectively L and R,
though they had, like nearly everybody
else, lost everything by the conflict, still
retained the high position in society which
they had for some long time filled. One of
them, the L, lost several of its members,
as well as its fortune, by the war, and at
the time of our story consisted of Mr.
L, gentleman 30 years of age, his wife,
nearly the same age, and an unmarried
daughter of about 15. Within about a
quarter of a mile of their house lived one
of the R, a young man who had recently
married a very beautiful young lady of the
county, and having left the paternal man-
sion, was farming by himself on a small
tract of ground. The two families lived
some distance from the county town, in
a sparsely inhabited section of country, and,
being each the nearest neighbor of the
other, were, of course, on terms of great
intimacy. Between the young wife and
the daughter of Mr. L, a fast friendship
was soon formed.


A few days since Mr. L informed his
wife that he had received a letter, which
would compel immediate attendance in At-
lanta, where he would have to remain several days, and as it would be inconvenient
for him to take her with him to that city,
he advised that she should ask her young
neighbor to stay with her during his ab-
sence. The next morning he set out in his
buggy for Atlanta, and his wife during the
morning went over to L for the purpose
of inviting her young friend to stay with her.
The young lady, after consultation with
her mother, readily assented to the propo-
sition, and promised to come over during
the afternoon.


About 8 o'clock Mrs. L began to feel a
little uneasy, as Miss L had not yet come,
when a servant came up to the house and
brought a note from her expected friend,
stating that she would be unable to spend
the night with her, as she had promised, for
her father, from some cause or other, had
positively refused to give his consent to the
arrangement. After delivering the note
the servant took his departure, and the
brave woman prepared to spend the night
by herself. Feeling that she had a protec-
tor in a large and very fierce yard-dog be-
longing to her husband, she took him into
her bedroom, and after securing the house
lay down and resigned herself to sleep.


About 11 o'clock she was awakened from
her slumbers by noise in the house and
the angry growling of the dog, and discov-
ered that the hall door had been forced,
and that some one was standing at her
room door, seeking an entrance. Speaking
as loudly as her fright would let her, Mrs.
L asked, "Who is there?" A man's voice, which she did not recognize, replied
by telling her to "open the door." Again
she asked the same question, and again re-
ceived the same answer, the stranger adding
that if she refused he would "break the
door down." During this dialogue the dog,
still growling, crouched upon the floor as if
ready to spring. Thinking to intimidate
this man, who sought her ruin, Mrs. L.
cried to him that if he forced the door she
would shoot him.


Laughing scornfully, the ruffian threw
his weight against the light door, burst it
open and entered the room—when, quick
as thought, the savage dog sprang forward
and fastened on his neck. The man gasped
at this sudden attack, attempted to kill
the animal with a knife which he held
in his hand, but unsuccessfully, and the
powerful animal dragged him to the
ground, still retaining his hold upon his
throat. Stunned at first by this, the woman,
in a few seconds, regaining her presence of mind some-
what, ran screaming from the house, never
stopping until she arrived at the place of
the L, where her cries soon aroused the
family.


Her tale was rapidly told, and the servants
were preparing to go to the scene of dan-
ger, when suddenly Mr. L was missed,
and his wife almost on the instant, as if
struck by a sudden presentiment, screamed
"Merciful God, it must be my husband!"
With a cry of horror the party set forth,
and ran as fast to the house of Mrs. R as
the latter had run away from it a few min-
utes before. Arrived there they found the
man still on the floor, and the dog still
grasping his throat. Beating him away
from his prey, they found the suspicions of
Mrs. L were not too correct, it was her husband;
but the teeth of the dog had done their
work, and he was dead.

THE DEAD SEA OF MoNo.-There are
many things in the Great Basin, or along
its rim, which excite the interest of travel
ers. A correspondent asks US to tell him
whether Mono Lake is actually the ''dead
sea" it is represented to be. am told that
its bitter water are fatal to all living things
If you can, will you say something about
that singular body of water" We gather
from the Report of the Mineral Resources
of the States and Territories west of the
Rocky Mountains" that Mono Lake lies
ten miles southwest of the dividing line be-
tween California and Nevada, and is about
fourteen miles long and nine wide. It has
never been sounded, but trial said to have
been made with line of three hundred feet
failed to reach the bottom. By chemical
analysis gallon of water weighing eight
pounds was found to contain !, 200 grains
of solid matter, consisting principally of
chloride of sodium, carbonate of soda, sui
phate of soda, borax and silica. These sub
stances render the water SO acid and nause-
ating that it is unfit for drinking or even
bathing. Leather immersed in it is soon
destroyed by its corrosive properties, and
not an animal, not even fish or frog can
exist in the water for more than short
time. The only thing able to live within or
upon the water of this lake is q species Of
fly, which springs from Larvae bred in its
bosom, and after an ephemeral life dies,
and collecting on the surface, is drifted to
the shore, where the remains collect in vast
quantities and are fed upon by the ducks or
gathered by the Indians, with whom they
are staple article OF food. Nesting under
the eastern watershed of the Sierra, Mono
Lake receives several considerable tributa-
ries and although destitute Of any outlet,
such is the aridity Of the atmosphere that
it is always kept at nearly uniform level
by the process of evaporation. So dense
and sluggish is the water rendered through
approximation with various salts and other
foreign matters, that only the strongest
winds raise ripple on its surface. AS the
Sierra in this neighborhood reaches nearly

no Lake is varied and majestic, some parts
of it being at the same time marked by a
more cheerless and desolate aspect. The
bitter and fatal waters Of this lake render it
literally dead sea, and its surroundings
wild, gloomy and foreboding-are sugges-
tive of sterility and death. The decompos-
ing action of the water is shown by its ef-
fects upon the bodies of a company OF In
dians, twenty to thirty in number, who,
while seeking TO escape from their white
pursuers, took refuge on the lake, where
they were shot by their enemies, who left
them in the water In the course Of few
weeks not vestige Of the bodies was to be

their lives were active as our own. They
passed like vapor, while Nature wore the
same aspect of beauty as when her Crea-
tor commanded her to be. The heavens
shall be as bright over our graves as they
now are around our path. Yet a little
while, and all will have happened. The
throbbing heart will be stilled and shall be
at rest. Our funeral will find its way, and
prayers will be said, and then we shall be
left alone in silence and darkness for the
worms. And it may be short time we
shall be spoken of, but the things of life
will creep in, and our names will soon be
forgotten. Days will continue to move on,
and song and laughter will be heard in the
room in which we died; and the eye
which mourned for us will be dried and
glisten again with joy, and even our chil-

not remember to lisp our names.

Provident Aid Society.

A regular meeting of the Board of Directors and officers of the Provident Aid Society was held last evening at the society's rooms, Dr. Peer Parker in the chair, and Col. James X. Brown secretary. Gen. Eaton having tendered to the society, free of charge, a quantity of desiccated vegetables, on motion of Mr. J. H. Johnson, the offer of Gen. Eaton was accepted. The Chair, from the committees appointed to wait upon the Mayor with regard to the distribution of the moneys appropriated by Congress for the poor of the District, stated in an interview with the Mayor that Gen. Eaton had expressed his inability to give any definite answer, the bill which had been passed had not yet been signed by the President, and it would be premature to take any action in the matter until the act became a law. He then took pleasure, however, in stating that the Mayor had expressed his friendship to the Provident Aid Society, and would place a reasonable proportion of the appropriation at its disposal. Mr. Alexander X. Shepherd inquired what report the committee appointed to wait upon the Mayor to ascertain the names of the parties who had been alleged had been guilty of improper conduct. Mr. J. H. Johnson replied that the committee had waited on the Mayor, who stated that the facts of the case were well known to the President and General Agent of the society. The President stated that the Mayor was entirely in error as regards his (the Chair's) knowledge of any dereliction of duty and improper conduct on the part of any member of the society. He had no knowledge of any such conduct: but there had been no testimony produced by which either of them could be convicted of any offence before Mr. A. X. Brown, said the Mayor had made complaints, which principally concerned some of the visitors of the society, but even these could not be regarded as offences; they were merely errors of judgment. The Chair stated that he did not think it worth while to pursue the subject any further, and then laid that the question to be considered was whether the society should exist any longer. Mr. Shepherd, treasurer, replied that he did think it could, as there was barely enough money in the treasury to meet the demands against the society. Mr. Solomons thought that, in view of the early prospect of a division of the appropriation made by Congress for the relief of the poor of the District the society should be continued; and sooner than its operations should now be suspended, he would himself be responsible for the expenses for one week. The President also hoped that the society would not suspend, and expressed his willingness to share the responsibility of expense with Mr. Solomons to keep it going one more week. On motion of Mr. Solomons, the Board then agreed to keep on another week. Resolutions offered by Mr. Solomons were adopted, that in view of the low condition of the funds in the treasury the visitors are requested to be very discreet in their distributions of aid to the poor hereafter, and that under further notice they be requested not to issue any recommendations for groceries to the Directors except in cases of great infirmity and old age. The General Agent said that it would not be necessary to make any appropriation for groceries as the Mayor would furnish the amount required for that object. Mr. Shepherd cautioned members against relying too much upon the appropriation by Congress. The amount donated would have to be divided between the Corporations of Washington, Georgetown, and the county of Washington. Besides, the intention of the appropriation was to give work to the indigent which, it is said, carried more good than by being given away. He moved that the General Agent be instructed to send written circulars to the ministers of all congregations in the city, requesting them to take collections on next Sabbath; carried. On motion of Mr. J. H. Johnson, the Agent was also instructed to have public notice inserted in the papers that these collections would be taken up in the different churches. The General Agent announced that the money had been expended in groceries, wood &c., and also that the Mayor had requested there should be no more issues until the bill making an appropriation for the poor was signed by the President of the United States. Adjourned.

THE FIFTH WARD POLITICALS.—Yesterday evening one of the Republican Clubs of the Fifth Ward (the Maryland wing, as it is called) held a meeting at the colored Baptist Church, on 4th street east, Capitol Hill. Horatio Maryman in the chair, and William H. Brown secretary. Mr. Sidney Herbert explained that he had been insulted by members of this club. He had never called the members of this club ruffians. Mr. William H. Brown said, "His name is Wm. H. Brown" and he thereby came there to get Mr. Brown to answer for it before the meeting, or retract it. Mr. Brown explained that he referred to Mr. Ananias Herbert, of Andrew Johnson's bread and butter brigade. Mr. Joseph Nicholson, chairman of the Vigilance Committee, submitted a resolution, which was adopted, affirming that this was the regularly organized club of the ward, that Horatio Maryman had been legally elected president of the club, and it was therefore duty to support him and protesting against the settlement of any difficulties outside the club room. When the resolutions were about to be put to a vote, a member objected. Wm. H. Brown said, "There goes firebrand from an office holder," he then proceeded to haul over in calls the ward representatives in the Councils, who had left out the colored schools in the appropriations and had voted with the Democrats, and no man could deny it. Authority being asked for this statement, Mr. Brown produced bound copies of the debates of the Councils to sustain his position. He then spoke of the meeting in Brown's Hall the other night, when club officers were elected, and if fifteen men could do that, why certainly two hundred and fifty men could do the same thing. The other party wanted to rule or ruin, but they were so dead that God Almighty would have to make a special resurrection in their behalf. While the members of the original club were fighting for their country, the men who compose the City Hall gang were here in the city with packs of cards in their pockets, cheating honorably discharged soldiers out of their money. The extracts from the Council debates which Mr. Brown had read were ordered to be printed. A proposition to appoint a committee of three to confer with the other clubs was voted down. The following delegates were appointed to attend the Workingmen's Convention at Union League Hall this evening: Wm. H. Brown, James Slower, Ed. X. Parker, J. J. Nicholson and John H. Shields. A motion that all present should sign the constitution of the club in order to be members caused a lengthy debate and great confusion which was gained by the entrance of Colonel Nenable of the sixth ward who, having just entered the room, was called on to address the meeting, which he did in harmony of action. A delegation from the other club appeared in front of the church about 10 o'clock with commotion, but all passed off quietly.

REPUBLICAN CENTRAL COMMITTEE.—The Republican General Committee of this city met yesterday evening at the office of Col. W. A. Cook, on 7th street. Colonel W. A. Cook, Chairman, and Benjamin N. Needs, Secretary. Resolutions were adopted recommending the Ward Clubs to take part in the inaugural procession; that they also appoint delegates to arrange for the reception of Senator Brownlow; and that a committee of seven be selected for the Central Committee to represent the interest. W. A. Cook, Cornelius Clark, H. A. Han, W. S. Morse, B. W. Needs, Henry Better and H. J. Johnson were chosen the committee and were instructed to urge upon Congress immediate action in relation to striking the word "white" from the charter of this city and all laws of Congress relating to the city, in accordance with the views expressed in the resolution of the Board of Aldermen. Adjourned.

its origin in the strong desire on the part of the loyal
people of the United States, of all classes and races,
to express in some worthy manner, their admira-
tion and gratitude for the patriotism, services in
his noble character of Abraham Lincoln, late president

liberty and humanity. In accordance with this pop-
ular feeling and to make it effectual, Congress
passed the law, which was approved by the Presi-
dent, incorporating the National Lincoln Monu-
ment Association, who duty it should be, under pro-
per organization, with rules and regulations, to pro-
ceed to collect funds and make all necessary plans
and arrangements to erect a suitable monument to
this great and good man somewhere within the pub-
lic grounds of the City of Washington.

the most prominent and honorable names

Driscoll of Michigan; for secretary, Hon. James H.
Edmonds, of the District of Columbia; for treas-
urer, Hon. J. W. Spinner, of the District of Colum-
bia.

description of the proposed monument:

The plan of this monument embraces in addi-
tion to the main column, groups of colossal
equestrian statues of the most prominent men in the history
for the preservation of the
Union; twenty-two colossal bronze statues of the
foremost statesmen, philanthropists and civilians
connected with the great contest; three groups of
colossal figures, representing the essential progress and abolition of slavery; and three figures
representing Time, Liberty and Justice; and all
six equestrian and thirty-two pedestals, and
colossal marble statues in basso-relievo depicting the
surrender of the Confederate
armies, and the United States Senate and House of
Representatives voting upon the amendment of the
constitution abolishing slavery and establishing
civil rights.

"For the equestrian statues the Board of Managers
has readily selected General W. S. Grant, Lieuten-
ant-General, Gen. W. T. Sherman, Gen. Y. W. Keyes,
and General James S. Wadsworth.

been determined upon: Hon. Salmon P. Chase,
Hon. Z. N. Stanton, Hon. Stephen A. Douglas and
Hon. W. H. Seward.

"Rev. Henry Ward Beecher and Rev. Matthew
Simpson as representatives of the loyal pulpit.

"As representatives of philanthropists the fol-
lowing gentlemen have been chosen: George S. Burnt,
President of the Christian Commission; Dr. W.
Fellows, President of the United States Sanitary
Commission; June Z. Yateman, President of the
Western Sanitary Commission.

"Three other names have been chosen as repre-
sentatives of the liberal arts.

They inform us that many other names are before
the board for consideration.

The cost of erecting the whole monument is estimated at
five hundred thousand dollars. To this Congress has generously appropriated
sufficient funds for the entire structure; thus
reducing the cost to the association to about one-half,
leaving about two hundred and fifty thousand dollars to be raised by appeals to the public and by indi-
vidual contributions.
